title: Care
hookLine: a planner filled in on day one, blank by week three; Shantideva's next chapter asks how a vow is kept
tomorrow: what keeps beating us, when it has no hands at all?

cards: Saturday morning, and a friend posts a photo in the group chat: a brand-new planner, every week color-coded, a promise to herself written on page one in her best handwriting. Everyone sends hearts.
A few weeks later the planner is under a pile of mail, open to a page that stays blank. Nobody broke that promise on purpose. It just wasn't guarded.
Shantideva knows this moment well. The vow he took yesterday is enormous, and his very next chapter starts right here: now that it's made, how does it stay alive?

teach.b: Chapter four of the poem is named for one word: apramada, care. Literally, not-careless.

teach.h: LETTING IT SLIDE DECEIVES THEM ALL.
teach.b: The opposite of letting it slide. Shantideva opens it plainly: having firmly taken hold of the awakening mind, a bodhisattva should strive never to stray from it. Then he gets blunt with himself.
He invited every being to happiness, out loud, before the Buddhas. If he lets that slide now, he says, he'd be deceiving them all. So the vow isn't a mood that comes and goes.
It's a promise with names on it. The Pali form of the same word is appamada, and the Dhammapada gives it a chapter of its own.

In Max Müller's old English, that chapter begins: "Earnestness is the path of immortality". Earnestness, care, heedfulness: translators reach for different words, and the picture underneath holds steady.

teach.h: A FLAME IN A WINDY YARD.
teach.b: A promise is like a small flame carried across a windy yard. Nobody blames the wind for being wind. You cup your hand.
That's the whole teaching of care. It isn't anxiety, and it isn't perfection. It's attention, again and again, to the thing you said you'd do.
The next pages name what tries to blow the flame out.

how: Some Mahayana Buddhists who have taken the bodhisattva vow renew it in their regular chanting, and Shantideva's chapter on care is studied as a guide to keeping that vow day to day.

o: keeping close watch so a promise doesn't slide
worrying about a task until it's done perfectly
being soft and gentle with everyone you meet

games.q: care, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: a promise made to every being
earnestness is the path of immortality

s: once a vow is taken, it keeps itself
Shantideva gives a whole chapter to guarding it: care.
Shantideva says letting his vow slide would deceive every being
he invited them all to happiness; dropping it would cheat them.
care here means worrying until everything is perfect
it means attention, again and again, to the thing you promised.

games.q: in june you promised your little cousin you'd teach her to ride a bike this summer. it's august. what does Shantideva's care look like now?
o: wait for a totally free weekend so you can do it properly.
put one short ride on the calendar this week, and show up.
tell her summer got busy, and promise again for next year.
games.why: care isn't a grand gesture someday. it's attention to the promise now, one small, guarded step at a time.

practice: Find a pen and anything to write on. Write one promise you've already made, small and real: to a friend, to your body, to yourself.
Under it, write the one next step that keeps it this week, and rest your eyes on the page while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Care: apramada, the opposite of careless. Shantideva's name for keeping a vow alive long after the moment of making it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: care, heedfulness, literally not-carelessness. In Pali the same word is appamada.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: guard the vow, the way you'd cup a flame in the wind. Chapter four, begun.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.1-4.6 (having firmly grasped the awakening mind, never stray from it; having invited all beings, to fail them would be to deceive them)
